english: Are all finite groups of linear transformations in arbitrarily many variables holoedrically isomorphic to a group of linear fractional substitutions in one variable, if one takes them congruent modulo a ...
topic: The page describes a function defined by inverting a ratio of solutions of a linear differential equation, invariant under the equation's monodromy group, compares it to Picard's functions, and then asks whether all finite groups of linear transformations are holoedrically isomorphic to groups of linear fractional substitutions in one variable.

triage.modern_statement: The note breaks off at 'congruent nach einem ...', so the last word is missing. The likeliest reading is 'modulo a prime (or prime power)'. On that reading the question is: is every finite group G of linear transformations, i.e. every finite subgroup of GL_n or PGL_n for any n, isomorphic ('holoedrically' means faithfully, as a true isomorphism) to a group of Möbius transformations z -> (az+b)/(cz+d) with coefficients taken mod p? In modern terms: does every finite group embed in PGL_2(F_q) for some prime power q, or equivalently in PGL_2 of the algebraic closure of F_p?
triage.answered_by: The answer is no. This follows from L. E. Dickson's classification of the subgroups of PSL_2(F_q) and PGL_2(F_q) (Linear Groups, 1901, §§239–261), building on Moore and Wiman. The finite subgroups of PGL_2(k) in characteristic p fall into a short list: cyclic groups, dihedral groups, A_4, S_4, A_5, PSL_2(q'), PGL_2(q'), and groups of the form elementary-abelian p-group extended by a cyclic group. Many finite groups are not on this list, for example A_7 or (C_2)^3. Faddeev and Beauville later extended the classification to an arbitrary field k.

evidence.claim: Dickson classified the subgroups of PSL_2(F) for finite fields F. Recent work gives a new proof and also characterizes the finite subgroups of PGL_2(F).
The finite subgroups of PGL_2(k) of order divisible by p go back to Dickson [Linear Groups, §239-261]. The classification has been completed up to conjugacy for any field k of characteristic p.
Dickson's theorem gives the complete list of maximal subgroups of PSL(2,q), for example C_q ⋊ C_{(q-1)/(2,q-1)} and dihedral groups. So the subgroups of PSL(2,q) are a narrow family.

triage.why: The note is cut off, but 'congruent nach einem [Primzahl]' points to linear fractional substitutions over Z/p or finite fields, a topic studied by Galois, Jordan, Klein, Moore and Dickson around 1890–1900. Dickson's classification answers the question in the negative. Only a few families of finite groups occur inside PGL_2 over a finite field or its algebraic closure. By contrast, every finite group sits inside some GL_n, using the permutation representation. None of the sources I found discuss Hilbert's note directly. This is not one of Hilbert's published problems. The classification itself is settled; current papers only re-prove it or extend it to arbitrary fields. Confidence is medium for two reasons: my reading of the missing final word is a guess, and the conclusion that the answer is no is my own reasoning from Dickson's list, not something the sources say about Hilbert's question.
